lessons.title: Course Introduction: From SQL Server DBA to Cross-Platform DBA
Why Organizations Run Multiple Database Platforms
Relational Concepts That Transfer vs. What Doesn't

slots.practicalActivity: Pull Docker images for an Oracle Database Free (23ai Free) container, mysql:8.0, and postgres:16 (don't run them yet) and confirm all three pulled successfully with `docker images`. Then draft a one-page comparison table with columns SQL Server | Oracle | MySQL | PostgreSQL and rows for process model, storage-structure terminology, default admin tool, and license model.
slots.deliverable: A `docker images` listing showing the oracle/database-free, mysql, and postgres images, plus a one-page markdown comparison table.

lessons.title: Comparing SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL & PostgreSQL at a Glance
Setting Up Your Cross-Platform Lab Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Stand up Oracle Database Free, MySQL 8, and PostgreSQL 16 containers side by side on distinct host ports (1521, 3306, 5432) with docker-compose, confirm all three are running with `docker ps`, and connect once to each with its native command-line client (sqlplus, mysql, psql) to prove connectivity.
slots.deliverable: A working docker-compose.yml running all three containers plus a terminal log showing a successful connection test to each.

lessons.title: Oracle Database Architecture: Instance vs. Database
Oracle Processes, Memory Structures & the SGA/PGA
Installing Oracle Database & Creating Your First Database

slots.practicalActivity: Connect to the Oracle container with `sqlplus / as sysdba`, query v$instance and v$sga to see the running instance name and SGA component sizes, then query v$process to count and identify the background processes (PMON, SMON, DBWn, LGWR) actually running.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output of the v$instance, v$sga, and v$process queries, annotated with what each background process does.

lessons.title: SQL*Plus, SQL Developer & Oracle Enterprise Manager

slots.practicalActivity: Inspect listener.ora and tnsnames.ora inside the Oracle container, run `lsnrctl status` to confirm the listener is up, create a new tablespace with its own datafile (CREATE TABLESPACE students_ts ...), and confirm it in DBA_TABLESPACES from both SQL*Plus and SQL Developer.
slots.deliverable: The `lsnrctl status` output plus the CREATE TABLESPACE script and a query proving the new tablespace exists.

slots.practicalActivity: Full install-and-verify lab: from a clean Oracle container, create a pluggable database, a tablespace, and a user/schema that owns objects in it, connect via SQL*Plus and SQL Developer, and run a join query across your own tables to prove the database is usable end to end.
slots.deliverable: A lab writeup with the CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE / CREATE TABLESPACE / CREATE USER statements and the working join query's output.

slots.practicalActivity: Create two Oracle users (app_read, app_write), create a role app_role granting SELECT on 3 tables and assign it to app_read, grant INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE directly to app_write, then create a PROFILE enforcing password expiration and resource limits and assign it to both users.
slots.deliverable: The CREATE USER / CREATE ROLE / GRANT / CREATE PROFILE scripts plus a DBA_ROLE_PRIVS and DBA_USERS query confirming the setup.

slots.practicalActivity: Enable unified auditing on one user's SELECT statements, run several queries as that user, and review UNIFIED_AUDIT_TRAIL for the captured activity. Separately, enable Transparent Data Encryption on one tablespace and confirm it via DBA_TABLESPACES / V$ENCRYPTED_TABLESPACES.
slots.deliverable: A UNIFIED_AUDIT_TRAIL query result showing captured statements, plus confirmation that the tablespace is TDE-encrypted.

lessons.title: Oracle Backup Fundamentals: Logical vs. Physical

slots.practicalActivity: Connect with `rman TARGET /`, run CONFIGURE RETENTION POLICY TO REDUNDANCY 2 and CONFIGURE CONTROLFILE AUTOBACKUP ON, take a full database backup followed by a level-1 incremental backup, and confirm both with LIST BACKUP SUMMARY.
slots.deliverable: An RMAN session log showing the CONFIGURE commands, both BACKUP commands, and the LIST BACKUP SUMMARY output.

slots.practicalActivity: Drop a table and recover it with FLASHBACK TABLE; separately corrupt a different schema's datafile and perform a full RMAN RESTORE/RECOVER; then export one schema with Data Pump (expdp) and import it into a different schema with impdp REMAP_SCHEMA.
slots.deliverable: Terminal logs for the FLASHBACK TABLE statement, the RMAN RESTORE/RECOVER session, and the expdp/impdp REMAP_SCHEMA run, each showing success.

slots.practicalActivity: Disaster-recovery lab: simulate a lost datafile while the database is down, bring the instance up, and walk the full RMAN RESTORE DATABASE / RECOVER DATABASE sequence to bring it back online, verifying row counts match before and after.
slots.deliverable: A written recovery runbook with every RMAN command used and a before/after row-count comparison proving no data loss.

lessons.title: Oracle Optimizer Statistics & the Cost-Based Optimizer

slots.practicalActivity: Run EXPLAIN PLAN FOR on a slow multi-table join, view it with DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY, identify a full table scan, then run DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS on the relevant tables and re-check whether the cost-based optimizer picks a different plan.
slots.deliverable: Before/after DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY output showing the plan change after gathering statistics.

slots.practicalActivity: Generate an AWR report (or query V$ACTIVE_SESSION_HISTORY) over a workload window, find the top SQL by elapsed time, create a B-tree index on the column driving its full table scan, and confirm the plan now uses an index range scan.
slots.deliverable: The AWR/ASH top-SQL excerpt, the CREATE INDEX statement, and the resulting execution plan.

slots.practicalActivity: Tuning lab: given 3 of your own slow queries, apply the full methodology — gather stats, read the plan, decide between an index or a rewrite — and record the before/after elapsed time for each.
slots.deliverable: A 3-query tuning report with before/after execution plans and timing for each query.

lessons.title: Oracle RAC: Real Application Clusters Overview

slots.practicalActivity: Using two Oracle containers, configure a physical standby database with Data Guard (force logging, standby control file, redo transport), and confirm redo apply is current with V$ARCHIVE_DEST_STATUS and V$DATAGUARD_STATS.
slots.deliverable: V$ARCHIVE_DEST_STATUS / V$DATAGUARD_STATS output proving redo apply is current on the standby.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a short decision memo on when GoldenGate's logical, trigger-based replication would be chosen over Data Guard's physical replication (e.g., mixed-version migration or selective table replication), and outline the concrete steps to upgrade your lab instance to the next patch level.
slots.deliverable: A one-page GoldenGate-vs-Data-Guard decision memo plus a step-by-step upgrade checklist.

slots.practicalActivity: Oracle wrap-up review: produce one working artifact for each of installation, security, backup/recovery, performance tuning, and high availability from your own lab environment, and confirm each still works.
slots.deliverable: An Oracle 'DBA readiness' checklist with command-plus-output evidence for all five areas.

lessons.title: MySQL Architecture: Server Layer vs. Storage Engine Layer
InnoDB vs. MyISAM & Choosing a Storage Engine

slots.practicalActivity: Connect to the MySQL container with the mysql CLI, create one table with ENGINE=InnoDB and one with ENGINE=MyISAM, insert rows into both, then kill the container ungracefully and restart it to see which table's data survives cleanly.
slots.deliverable: A short write-up comparing the post-crash state of the InnoDB vs. MyISAM table in terms of crash recovery and the redo log.

slots.practicalActivity: Edit my.cnf to change a system variable (e.g., innodb_buffer_pool_size), restart MySQL, confirm with SHOW VARIABLES LIKE, then connect with both the mysql CLI and MySQL Workbench and run an identical query in each.
slots.deliverable: SHOW VARIABLES output confirming the change, plus a Workbench export matching the CLI's results.

slots.practicalActivity: Full MySQL install-and-configure lab: install/reset MySQL, harden the root account, set 3 meaningful configuration variables for a small production-like workload, create a schema with at least 2 InnoDB tables, and connect successfully from Workbench and the CLI.
slots.deliverable: A lab report listing each configuration change and why, plus proof of successful connections from both tools.

slots.practicalActivity: Create two host-scoped MySQL users (app_user@'10.%' and report_user@'localhost'), create a role report_role with SELECT-only grants on 2 tables and assign it to report_user, and confirm each account's real privileges with SHOW GRANTS.
slots.deliverable: The CREATE USER / CREATE ROLE / GRANT scripts plus SHOW GRANTS output for both accounts.

lessons.title: Encryption at Rest & in Transit in MySQL

slots.practicalActivity: Apply at least 3 hardening steps (remove anonymous accounts, disable remote root, require SSL for one user), then enable encryption at rest for one table (innodb_file_per_table + keyring) and confirm an SSL-encrypted client connection with `\s` in the mysql CLI.
slots.deliverable: A hardening checklist with before/after evidence plus the mysql CLI `\s` output proving the SSL-encrypted connection.

lessons.title: MySQL Backup Strategies: Logical vs. Physical

slots.practicalActivity: Take a logical backup of one schema with `mysqldump --single-transaction` (including routines/triggers), then a physical hot backup of the data directory with Percona XtraBackup, and compare the two backups' size and restore time.
slots.deliverable: The mysqldump and xtrabackup commands, the resulting backup artifacts, and a size/restore-time comparison.

slots.practicalActivity: Enable binary logging, make several writes, simulate an accidental DELETE at a known timestamp, then perform point-in-time recovery by restoring the last full backup and replaying binlog events up to just before the bad DELETE with mysqlbinlog.
slots.deliverable: The mysqlbinlog replay command and a verification query proving the deleted rows are back with no later data lost.

slots.practicalActivity: Disaster-recovery lab: starting only from a mysqldump backup and the binary logs, rebuild the database to a point five minutes before a simulated failure, verifying row counts and sample rows against the pre-disaster state.
slots.deliverable: A recovery runbook with every command run and a before/after row-count and sample-data verification.

slots.practicalActivity: Run EXPLAIN on a slow multi-table JOIN, identify a full table scan (type: ALL), add a covering index, and re-run EXPLAIN to confirm the type changes to ref/range with far fewer rows examined.
slots.deliverable: Before/after EXPLAIN output and the CREATE INDEX statement that fixed the scan.

lessons.title: The MySQL Performance Schema & sys Schema
Configuration Tuning: Buffer Pool & Key Variables

slots.practicalActivity: Query performance_schema/sys schema views (e.g., sys.statements_with_full_table_scans) to find a real tuning opportunity in your schema, then adjust innodb_buffer_pool_size based on your dataset's working-set size and confirm with SHOW VARIABLES.
slots.deliverable: The sys-schema query identifying the issue, plus the buffer-pool size change and confirmation output.

slots.practicalActivity: Tuning lab: given 3 of your own slow queries, apply methodology → EXPLAIN → sys-schema diagnostics → an indexing or config fix for each, recording the elapsed-time improvement.
slots.deliverable: A 3-query tuning report with before/after timings and the specific fix applied to each.

slots.practicalActivity: Using two MySQL containers, configure GTID-based source-replica replication, confirm SHOW REPLICA STATUS reports both IO and SQL threads running on the replica, then write to the source and confirm the row appears on the replica.
slots.deliverable: SHOW REPLICA STATUS output plus proof that a row written on the source replicated to the replica.

slots.practicalActivity: Install MySQL Router in front of the source-replica pair, configure it to route writes to the source and reads to the replica, and confirm with two separate connections; separately outline the concrete steps to upgrade your lab's MySQL version.
slots.deliverable: Connection-test output proving Router splits write and read traffic correctly, plus a written upgrade plan.

slots.practicalActivity: High-availability lab: promote the replica to source (stop replication, reconfigure it as the new source) and confirm the application-facing connection via Router can still read and write afterward.
slots.deliverable: A failover runbook with each step and a final proof that reads/writes succeed against the newly promoted source.

slots.practicalActivity: Query pg_stat_activity in the PostgreSQL container to see the running backend processes, then edit postgresql.conf to change shared_buffers and pg_hba.conf to allow a new host/user combination, reload with `SELECT pg_reload_conf();`, and confirm both changes.
slots.deliverable: pg_stat_activity output plus confirmation that the new pg_hba.conf rule and changed shared_buffers value are active.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a tablespace on a second path, create a schema in it, confirm from both psql and pgAdmin that it exists, then install one real extension (pg_stat_statements or pgcrypto) with CREATE EXTENSION and confirm it in pg_extension.
slots.deliverable: The CREATE TABLESPACE / CREATE SCHEMA / CREATE EXTENSION scripts plus a pg_extension query confirming the extension.

slots.practicalActivity: Full PostgreSQL install-and-configure lab: install PostgreSQL from scratch, configure pg_hba.conf for a new application role, build a database/schema/tablespace layout for a small app, and connect successfully from psql and pgAdmin.
slots.deliverable: A lab report with the full configuration applied and proof of successful connections from both tools.

slots.practicalActivity: Create two roles (app_read, app_write) with appropriate GRANTs, then enable Row-Level Security on one table with a policy restricting each role to only its own tenant's rows, and prove it by querying as each role.
slots.deliverable: The CREATE ROLE / GRANT / CREATE POLICY scripts plus query output proving RLS restricts each role's visible rows.

slots.practicalActivity: Install pgAudit, configure it to log DDL and role-changing statements, trigger a few, and review the log; separately configure SSL for client connections and confirm an encrypted psql connection with sslmode=require.
slots.deliverable: The pgAudit log excerpt showing captured statements, plus proof of an SSL-encrypted psql connection.

lessons.title: PostgreSQL Backup Strategies: pg_dump vs. Physical Backups

slots.practicalActivity: Take a logical backup of one database with `pg_dump -Fc`, a full-cluster logical backup with `pg_dumpall --globals-only`, and a physical base backup of the cluster with pg_basebackup, then compare restore steps for each.
slots.deliverable: The pg_dump / pg_dumpall / pg_basebackup commands used plus a short comparison of what each restores and how.

slots.practicalActivity: Enable WAL archiving, take a base backup, make several writes, simulate an accidental data-destroying statement, then recover to a target time just before it with recovery_target_time and verify the bad statement's effects are gone.
slots.deliverable: The recovery_target_time configuration and a verification query proving PITR landed at the correct point.

slots.practicalActivity: Disaster-recovery lab: starting only from a pg_basebackup and archived WAL, rebuild the cluster to a specific point in time, verifying row counts and sample rows against the expected pre-disaster state.
slots.deliverable: A recovery runbook with every command run and a before/after verification of row counts and sample data.

slots.practicalActivity: Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on a slow multi-table join, identify a Seq Scan with high actual time, add an index, and re-run to confirm the plan now uses an Index Scan with lower actual time.
slots.deliverable: Before/after EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) output and the CREATE INDEX statement.

slots.practicalActivity: Generate table bloat with repeated UPDATE/DELETE cycles, confirm it via pg_stat_user_tables (n_dead_tup), run VACUUM, then enable pg_stat_statements to find your most time-consuming query and tune shared_buffers based on your lab's available memory.
slots.deliverable: pg_stat_user_tables before/after VACUUM output, plus the pg_stat_statements query and the shared_buffers change.

slots.practicalActivity: Tuning lab: given 3 of your own slow queries, apply methodology → EXPLAIN ANALYZE → an indexing or VACUUM/config fix for each, recording the elapsed-time improvement.
slots.deliverable: A 3-query tuning report with before/after timings and the specific fix applied to each.

slots.practicalActivity: Using two PostgreSQL containers, configure physical streaming replication (primary_conninfo, a replication slot, hot_standby), confirm it's active with pg_stat_replication/pg_stat_wal_receiver, then set up logical replication for one table and confirm rows replicate.
slots.deliverable: pg_stat_replication / pg_stat_wal_receiver output proving streaming is active, plus proof a row replicated via logical replication.

slots.practicalActivity: Install PgBouncer in transaction-pooling mode in front of the primary and confirm with SHOW POOLS that client connections are pooled down to fewer backend connections; separately write out the pg_upgrade steps for your lab cluster.
slots.deliverable: PgBouncer SHOW POOLS output demonstrating pooling, plus a written pg_upgrade plan.

slots.practicalActivity: High-availability lab: promote the streaming replica to primary with `pg_ctl promote` (simulating a primary failure) and confirm the application-facing connection can read and write against the new primary.
slots.deliverable: A failover runbook with the promotion steps and a final proof that reads/writes succeed against the new primary.

lessons.title: Migrating SQL Server to Oracle: Key Differences
Migrating SQL Server to PostgreSQL: Key Differences

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a real small SQL Server schema (e.g., Person and Sales from AdventureWorks) and write a migration assessment covering object count and feature gaps, with a separate data-type mapping table for an Oracle target and a PostgreSQL target.
slots.deliverable: A written migration-assessment document with two data-type mapping tables (SQL Server→Oracle, SQL Server→PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Migrating SQL Server to MySQL: Key Differences
Data Type Mapping & Schema Conversion Across Platforms
ETL & Data Migration Tools for Cross-Platform Moves

slots.practicalActivity: Extend the mapping table with a SQL Server→MySQL column, convert and recreate 2-3 of the assessed tables' DDL for one chosen target platform, and use a real migration tool (pgloader, Ora2Pg, or AWS DMS free tier) to move sample rows across.
slots.deliverable: The converted CREATE TABLE DDL for the chosen target plus a row-count match proving sample data migrated successfully.

slots.practicalActivity: Full migration lab: migrate the same small schema end to end into a different target platform than the one just practiced, documenting every data type translated and every SQL Server feature worked around.
slots.deliverable: A migration runbook for the full schema move, including a final source-vs-target row-count verification.

lessons.title: Project Introduction — You're the Cross-Platform DBA
Project — Standing Up Oracle, MySQL & PostgreSQL Side by Side

slots.practicalActivity: Read the capstone brief (you're the sole cross-platform DBA for a company running Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL), then stand up all three fresh with the same small customers/orders schema ported into each platform's native DDL.
slots.deliverable: Three running databases (Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL), each with the same customers/orders schema in that platform's native DDL.

lessons.title: Project — Securing & Backing Up All Three Platforms

slots.practicalActivity: On each of the three platforms, create at least one restricted role/user and take one backup using that platform's native tool (RMAN, mysqldump/XtraBackup, pg_dump/pg_basebackup), documenting the security-and-backup posture side by side.
slots.deliverable: A security-and-backup comparison matrix (one row per platform) with the actual commands run and backup artifacts produced.

slots.practicalActivity: Run the same multi-table join-with-filter query pattern against all three platforms' copy of the schema, capture each platform's execution plan, and tune each with that platform's own indexing approach, recording before/after timing for all three.
slots.deliverable: A three-way performance comparison report with before/after execution plans and timings for Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL.

slots.practicalActivity: Write your own answers to 8 realistic cross-platform DBA interview questions covering architecture differences, backup/recovery tooling, and migration pitfalls, then do a timed mock interview answering 3 of them aloud without notes.
slots.deliverable: A written Q&A document for 8 interview questions plus notes from the timed mock-interview run.

lessons.title: Course Wrap-Up: Choosing Where to Specialize Next

slots.practicalActivity: Reflect in writing on which platform felt closest to your existing SQL Server DBA instincts and which felt most different, then pick one specialization track to research further with 3 concrete next resources.
slots.deliverable: A one-page specialization reflection naming a chosen next-focus platform and 3 concrete resources to pursue it.

slots.practicalActivity: Final capstone build-out: add one more realistic requirement to the 3-platform project (a MySQL reporting replica, an Oracle Data Guard standby, or RLS-restricted PostgreSQL reporting access), implement it on all three, and write an operations runbook a teammate could follow.
slots.deliverable: A finished 3-platform operations runbook plus proof (commands + output) that the new requirement is implemented on each platform.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can install, secure, back up, tune, and replicate real databases on Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL, and can assess and execute a cross-platform migration from SQL Server to any of the three.
